Fig. 1. Overview of this work. Autonomous driving scenarios incorporating the states of observed vehicles and time to collision are sampled from 
the state set. These scenarios train a deep reinforcement learning network that solves a partition problem. After rigorous veriﬁcation, the network 
establishes a provable unsafe set partition wherein each subset contains states sharing the same minimum steps to collision. This partition is then 
instantiated into the provable minimum collision time as a safety metric, and a provable upper bond of the system collision risk.

Fig. 2. The Veriﬁcation Process of the Q Network. For each veriﬁcation iteration, the initial state is ﬁrst randomly sampled from the feasible set. 
The true collision step count is determined through simulation run in simulator, while the Q network constructed with encoder and value function 
provides a corresponding prediction by rounding the output. If the true value falls below the predicted value, indicating non-compliance with the 
veriﬁcation theorem, the process terminates and reverts to training. Otherwise, veriﬁcation continues until the number of successful trials satisﬁes 
the theorem’s requirements.

Fig. 3. Settings of the autonomous driving system. The experiments are conducted in a three-lane highway environment, where each lane is 
1200 meters long and 4 meters wide, with longitudinal axes aligned along the x-axis. The autonomous vehicle continuously monitors the kinematic 
states of six critical background vehicles within a circular observation zone of 118-meter radius. These background vehicles are designated as the 
leading, following, left-leading, left-following, right-leading, and right-following background vehicles, with external vehicles randomly generated 
according to the naturalistic driving environment.

Fig. 4. Comparison between predicted collision times and true values. The histogram on the left compares collision times predicted by PMCT 
against ground-truth values. The x-axis represents binned predicted collision times, with the y-axis indicating sample counts. Green bars denote 
instances where ground-truth collision time ≥ predicted value, while purple bars indicate failure cases where ground-truth collision time < predicted 
value. Red dashed lines delineate the predetermined misclassiﬁcation rate threshold for the failure data. The line chart on the right details the 
misclassiﬁcation rate corresponding to each predicted collision time bin. This empirical distribution validates compliance with the theoretical 
misclassiﬁcation rate threshold.

Fig. 5. ROC curve and PR curve of the safety metrics. The left ﬁgure presents the ROC curve, and the right one presents the PR curve. The 
subgraph in the PR curve ﬁgure is a magniﬁed view focusing exclusively on the high-recall (0.85 to 1.00) threshold. Results demonstrate that PMCT 
can achieve a relatively high Recall unattainable by alternative metrics, and maintain substantially higher precision at equivalent Recall levels.

Fig. 6. Snapshots and collision time predictions of two real-time collision scenarios. In subﬁgures (a) and (b), AV executes rightward and 
leftward lane changes, respectively, subsequently colliding with the leading BV in the target lane. In each subﬁgure, snapshots show the scenario’s 
initial state, lane-changing maneuver and collision state, with longitudinal position and lane index represented on the x-axis and y-axis respectively. 
Line charts present the collision time predictions by three safety metrics at each time step compared with the actual remaining time to the colli-
sion step. Results demonstrate that PMCT outperforms other two metrics in successfully predicting a shorter collision time than the actual value, 
facilitating timely human intervention in high-risk scenarios through earlier collision alerts.

Fig. 7. Mcity digital twin in TeraSim and examples of collision types. (a) An overview of Mcity. (b) A rear-end collision occurred on a straight 
road. (c) A cut-in collision occurred at an intersection. (d) A head-on collision occurred at an intersection. (e) A roundabout rear-end collision caused 
by delayed braking of the rear car.

Fig. 9. ROC curve and PR curve of the safety metrics on the test sets for road and intersection collision scenarios. Sub-ﬁgure (a) shows the 
result on the test set of road collision scenarios, and sub-ﬁgure (b) shows the result on the test set of intersection collision scenarios. In each sub-
ﬁgure, the left line chart presents the ROC curve, and the right one presents the PR curve. Results demonstrate that PMCT can achieve a relatively 
high Recall unattainable by alternative metrics, and maintain substantially higher precision at equivalent Recall levels on both test sets.

Fig. 10. Trajectories of real-world collision scenarios from ROCO. The ﬁgure illustrates three distinct accident cases , where blue and red 
trajectories represent the two primary vehicles involved in each conﬂict. The gradient of the color indicates the temporal progression. Lighter 
shades mark the starting positions, while darker shades denote the concluding positions of the sequence. Rectangular markers represent the vehicle 
poses at discrete time steps with a frequency of 2.5𝐻𝑧, and black circles highlight the exact spatial locations where the collisions occurred.

Fig. 11. Collision time predictions of real-time collision scenarios. Each sub-ﬁgure illustrates the safety metric prediction results for a speciﬁc 
accident, where both involved vehicles are sequentially treated as the ego vehicle across the selected temporal slices. The two prediction results are 
shown as line charts, and each line chart presents the collision time predictions by three safety metrics at each time step compared with the actual 
remaining time to the collision step.
